mainTopic: Permitting a בכור and releasing a נדר without an expert, refunds for sold food that turns out to be forbidden, and, opening a new פרק, which blemishes permit slaughtering a בכור.
overview: The גמרא finishes explaining that three ordinary people may permit a בכור when no expert is available, which rejects רבי יוסי. In the same way, three people may release a נדר when no חכם is available, which rejects רבי יהודה. רב rules that the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי. The גמרא tries to use this to prove that an earlier ruling was שמואל's, but that proof is rejected. A new משנה then covers a seller whose meat turns out to be a בכור that was never checked, or a טרפה, and explains how money and meat are returned. A ברייתא adds רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's view: for food people find disgusting, the seller refunds everything. For food people enjoy, he deducts its value. The גמרא shows that the seller really lost something in each case of בכור, טבל, and יין נסך. After the הדרן, a new פרק opens with a list of ear blemishes that permit slaughtering a בכור. The גמרא begins deriving from the פסוק, using כלל ופרט וכלל, which blemishes count, and that discussion continues on the next עמוד.

steps.title: The ruling about three laymen rejects רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: The ruling that three ordinary people may permit a בכור where there is no מומחה excludes the view of רבי יוסי in the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: This ruling comes to exclude the view of רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing its explanation of a ruling from the previous עמוד: three regular people can permit a בכור (declare its blemish permanent) when no expert is around. It tells us which opinion this ruling argues against.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, רבי יוסי holds that only an expert (מומחה) can permit a בכור. Even a court of twenty-three ordinary judges cannot do it. The ruling of 'three where there is no expert' therefore deliberately disagrees with רבי יוסי.

keyTerms.meaning: To exclude; this comes to reject a certain opinion
A firstborn kosher animal, holy to the כהן; it may be eaten only if it has a permanent blemish
A recognized expert in judging blemishes

steps.confusionAlert: This line has no subject of its own. It is the tail end of the ruling quoted at the end of the previous עמוד: 'three may permit a בכור where there is no expert.'

phrases.english: to exclude [the view] of Rabbi Yosei,
phrases.notes: Refers back to the ruling on 36b about three laymen permitting a firstborn.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ruling from the end of 36b.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Three laymen may permit a בכור where no מומחה exists, against רבי יוסי.

steps.title: Three people may annul a vow where there is no Sage
steps.stepSummary: A parallel ruling: three ordinary people can release a נדר in a place where no חכם is available.
steps.simpleTranslation: Three people may annul a vow in a place where there is no Sage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second ruling with the same structure, this time about vows. If no חכם is around, a group of three may release someone from a נדר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling is built like the בכור ruling: an expert is ideal, and three ordinary people act as a substitute when no expert is available. The wording 'where there is no חכם' implies that a real חכם could do it alone.

keyTerms.meaning: Annul or release (here: releasing a person from a vow)
A vow
A Sage; a Torah scholar qualified to release vows

phrases.english: Three may annul the vow
phrases.notes: Here the word means releasing a vow by a court (התרה), not a husband's or father's הפרה.

phrases.english: in a place where there is no Sage.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלֹשָׁה מְפִירִין אֶת הַנֶּדֶר בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁאֵין חָכָם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel ruling with the same structure as the בכור ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Where no חכם is available, three people may release a נדר.

steps.title: The vow ruling rejects רבי יהודה
steps.stepSummary: The vow ruling excludes רבי יהודה, who requires that one of the three be a חכם, as a ברייתא teaches.
steps.simpleTranslation: This comes to exclude the view of רבי יהודה, as a ברייתא teaches: Releasing vows needs three. רבי יהודה says: one of them must be a Sage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains which opinion the vow ruling argues against. It quotes a ברייתא where רבי יהודה demands that at least one of the three be a חכם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to רבי יהודה, three complete laymen are never enough; a חכם must be among them. The ruling 'three where there is no חכם' allows three non-חכמים, so it rejects רבי יהודה.

keyTerms.meaning: As it was taught in a ברייתא
Releasing or annulling vows

phrases.english: to exclude [the view] of Rabbi Yehuda,
as it is taught: Annulment of vows is with three;

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶם חָכָם.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: one of them must be a Sage.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Names the opposing view to the ruling in step 2 and gives its source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The vow ruling disagrees with רבי יהודה, who requires a חכם among the three.
steps.whatToRemember: Both rulings follow one pattern. An expert is best. Without one, three ordinary people suffice. This rejects רבי יוסי (for בכור) and רבי יהודה (for vows).

steps.title: Who counts as the Sage meant here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: who is an example of the kind of חכם who could release a vow alone?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'In a place where there is no Sage' — for example, who?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the phrase 'where there is no חכם.' It wants to know what level of scholar counts as a חכם who could act alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase implies that a real חכם can release a vow by himself. So the גמרא needs to define how great someone must be to qualify. Without that, we don't know when the three-layman option applies.

keyTerms.meaning: For example, who?

phrases.english: 'In a place where there is no Sage.'
Such as whom?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Clarifies a term in the vow ruling.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The definition of the חכם who may release vows alone.

steps.title: רב נחמן: someone like me
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן answers that a חכם is someone of his own stature.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Someone like me.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן answers the question. A חכם who can release vows alone is a recognized expert at his own level.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב נחמן was a leading judge and authority, so the standard is high: a widely recognized expert (יחיד מומחה). An ordinary learned person does not qualify to act alone.

keyTerms.meaning: Someone like me
A leading אמורא and judge in בבל

phrases.english: Rav Nachman said: Such as me.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A חכם is a top-level recognized expert, like רב נחמן.

steps.title: Can the other two be anyone at all?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה requires only one חכם. Does that mean the other two can be totally unlearned?
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רבי יהודה says: one of them must be a Sage.' Does that imply that the others can be just anyone?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי יהודה's words in the ברייתא and draws an inference. If only one must be a חכם, maybe the other two can be complete ignoramuses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Reading רבי יהודה literally, he requires only one qualified member. The גמרא questions whether that is really true, since it seems odd that totally ignorant people could sit on such a court.

keyTerms.meaning: By implication; this implies that
Anyone at all, whoever

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: אֶחָד מֵהֶן חָכָם,
phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yehuda says: one of them must be a Sage' —
by implication, those [others] can be anyone?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to רבי יהודה's view from step 3 to clarify it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What are the minimum qualifications of the other two members?

steps.title: They must be able to understand when it is explained
steps.stepSummary: רבינא: the other members must be people who can understand the laws of vows once they are explained to them.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said: People to whom it is explained and they understand.
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא answers that the other two cannot be just anyone. They must be capable of understanding the laws of vows when someone explains them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a middle level between a חכם and a total ignoramus. The other two need not be scholars, but they must be able to grasp the reasoning when taught. This keeps the court meaningful.

keyTerms.meaning: That when it is explained to him, he understands
A late אמורא

phrases.english: Ravina said: [People] to whom it is explained and he understands.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 6.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The other members must be able to understand the הלכות when explained.

steps.title: רב rules: the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי
steps.stepSummary: Quoting the משנה's view of רבי יוסי, רב חננאל reports in the name of רב that the הלכה does not follow רבי יוסי.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'רבי יוסי says: Even if there are twenty-three there, etc.' רב חננאל said in the name of רב: The הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה's quote from רבי יוסי, who says only an expert can permit a בכור, even if twenty-three judges are present. רב rules that we do not follow רבי יוסי.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is a practical ruling. In practice, ordinary people may permit a בכור when no מומחה is available, against רבי יוסי. The גמרא will next ask why this ruling was needed at all.

keyTerms.meaning: Twenty-three, the size of a סנהדרין קטנה
The practical law is not (like this view)
Etc.; the quote continues

phrases.english: 'Rabbi Yosei says:

phrases.aramaic: אֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ שָׁם עֶשְׂרִים וּשְׁלֹשָׁה כּוּ׳.
phrases.english: even if there are twenty-three there, etc.'
phrases.notes: Quoting the משנה: even so, it may be slaughtered only on an expert's word.

phrases.english: Rav Chananel said in the name of Rav:
The halakha is not like Rabbi Yosei.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב חֲנַנְאֵל אָמַר רַב: אֵין הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic on the משנה's words of רבי יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה does not follow רבי יוסי regarding permitting a בכור.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious? The majority wins
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: there is a rule that the הלכה follows the many against one, so why did רב need to say this?
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious! Between one and many, the הלכה follows the many!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב's ruling as unnecessary. רבי יוסי is a lone opinion against the majority, and we always follow the majority anyway.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a general rule: יחיד ורבים הלכה כרבים. Since רבי יוסי disagrees with the תנא קמא (the majority view), the outcome seems automatic. So רב's statement seems to add nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: It is obvious!
Between an individual and the many, the law follows the many

phrases.english: It is obvious! [In a dispute of] an individual and the many, the halakha is like the many!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רב's ruling.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's statement that the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The general majority rule already gives this result, so the statement seems redundant.

steps.title: Needed because רבי יוסי's reasoning is usually followed
steps.stepSummary: One might think רבי יוסי is an exception because his reasoning is always sound (נמוקו עמו), so רב teaches that here we still do not follow him.
steps.simpleTranslation: You might have said: his reasoning is with him. So it teaches us otherwise.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. רבי יוסי has a special reputation, and that could have led us to follow him even against the majority. רב's statement blocks that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a known principle: רבי יוסי נמוקו עמו, meaning his opinions are well-grounded, and we often follow him. Without רב's ruling, we might have applied that here and overridden the majority rule. רב tells us that in this case the majority rule stands.

keyTerms.meaning: You might have said
His reasoning is with him; his views are well-founded
It teaches us (otherwise)

phrases.english: You might have said: his reasoning is with him;
[therefore] it teaches us [that it is not so].

steps.triggerLanguage: מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא נִמּוּקוֹ עִמּוֹ? קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Shows the statement is needed to block a mistaken assumption (מהו דתימא)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Because רבי יוסי נמוקו עמו, we might follow him even against the majority.
steps.terutzMaskana: In this case the majority rule applies, and the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי.

steps.title: So the first ruling must have been שמואל's
steps.stepSummary: Because רב himself ruled against רבי יוסי, the earlier ruling (three permit a בכור, against רבי יוסי) must have been said in the name of שמואל. Otherwise רב would have said the same thing twice.
steps.simpleTranslation: Resolve from this that the first ruling was said in the name of שמואל. For if it was in the name of רב, why would I need two?
steps.whatsHappening: The previous עמוד was unsure whether the 'three may permit a בכור' ruling was in the name of רב or שמואל. The גמרא now tries to use רב's ruling here to settle that doubt. The next step rejects this proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both statements reach the same result: the הלכה is not like רבי יוסי. One person would not need to say the same thing twice. Since this ruling is clearly רב's, the earlier one must belong to שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Resolve (the doubt)
The first one (the earlier ruling)
Why would I need two (identical statements)?

steps.whatToRemember: The הלכה is not like רבי יוסי. Ordinary people may permit a בכור where there is no מומחה, and רב says this explicitly. The attempt to prove that the earlier ruling was שמואל's is rejected in the next step.

phrases.english: Resolve from this
that that first [ruling] was stated in the name of Shmuel,
for if [it was] in the name of Rav —
why do I need two?

steps.triggerLanguage: תִּפְשׁוֹט מֵהָא, דְּהָךְ קַמַּיְיתָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל אִיתְּמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses רב's ruling from step 8 to resolve the attribution doubt from 36b.
steps.raayaObject: Who said the earlier ruling (רב or שמואל)
steps.raayaSupportSource: רב's explicit ruling here; a single אמורא would not repeat the same ruling twice

steps.title: Maybe one ruling was only inferred from the other
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof from step 11. רב may have said only one ruling out loud, and the second was reported in his name as an inference from the first.
steps.simpleTranslation: One of the two rulings was said by inference from the other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא knocks down the proof from step 11. It says רב did not have to say the same thing twice: he said it once, and the second version was worked out from the first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 11 argued that the בכור ruling had to come from שמואל, since otherwise רב repeated himself. The answer here is that רב said only one statement. His students drew the second one out of it and quoted it in his name. Since nothing was actually repeated, the proof fails, and the בכור ruling could still be רב's.

keyTerms.meaning: One (of the two statements)
By inference; drawn out of a general statement
Of its fellow; from the other statement
It was stated or reported

steps.whatToRemember: A report in a teacher's name may be an inference his students drew, not words he actually said. So 'he wouldn't say it twice' is not always a proof.
steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean anyone made up a ruling. The second report is a correct inference from what רב really said.

phrases.english: One was by inference
phrases.notes: The parentheses and brackets show a text correction: the older reading מכלל is replaced with מִכְּלָלָא.

phrases.english: from the other, it was stated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in step 11
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof that the בכור ruling must be שמואל's. It does not affect the הלכה against רבי יוסי.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed רב said both statements explicitly. One could be an inference his students reported in his name.

steps.title: Selling meat of a firstborn that was never shown to an expert
steps.stepSummary: New משנה: someone slaughtered a בכור and sold the meat without first showing the animal to an expert. He must refund the buyers, both for what they ate and for what is left. The leftover meat must be buried.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone slaughters a firstborn animal, and it becomes known that he did not show it to an expert: what the buyers ate, they ate, and he must return the money to them. As for what they did not eat, the meat must be buried, and he must return the money.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on a seller who sold meat from a בכור without having an expert confirm that the animal had a real מום.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור may only be slaughtered and eaten outside the Temple once an expert confirms it has a מום. Without that check, the meat is forbidden even for benefit. So the leftover meat cannot be sold or used and must be buried. The seller refunds the buyers for everything, even the meat they already ate, as a penalty on him.

keyTerms.meaning: Abbreviation for מַתְנִיתִין, our משנה
Firstborn animal
He showed it (to an expert, to confirm a blemish)
Must be buried
Money; the purchase price

steps.whyThisMatters: The seller is responsible for the buyers' loss even though they already ate the meat. This sets up the comparison with the טרפה case that follows.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who slaughters the firstborn,
and it became known that he did not show it (to an expert) —
what they ate, they ate,
and he must return the money to them,
and what they did not eat —
the meat must be buried,
and he must return the money.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַבְּכוֹר וְנוֹדַע שֶׁלֹּא הֶרְאָהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה and a new topic
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Seller of an unchecked בכור refunds all the money. The uneaten meat is buried.

steps.title: Selling a cow that turns out to be a טרפה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה moves to a second case, a cow that turns out to be a טרפה. Leftover meat goes back to the seller and he refunds the buyers. If the buyers already sold it to gentiles or fed it to dogs, they pay him the lower value of טרפה meat.
steps.simpleTranslation: Likewise, if someone slaughters a cow and sells it, and it becomes known that it is a טרפה: what they ate, they ate. As for what they did not eat, they return the meat to him, and he returns the money to them. If they sold it to gentiles or threw it to dogs, they pay the value of טרפה meat.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה gives a parallel case: meat from a cow that turns out to be a טרפה. It explains how the money and the meat are settled between buyer and seller.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike a בכור, a טרפה may still be used for benefit, for example sold to a gentile or fed to dogs. So the leftover meat is not buried. It goes back to the seller, and he refunds the price. If the buyers already got some use out of it, they pay only what טרפה meat is worth, which is less than kosher meat, and the seller refunds the difference.

keyTerms.meaning: An animal with a fatal defect, forbidden to eat but allowed for benefit
Cow
They threw it to the dogs
The price of טרפה meat (lower than kosher meat)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not confuse this with the בכור case. There the meat is buried because no benefit at all is allowed. Here the meat still has value because a טרפה may be used for benefit.

phrases.english: And likewise, one who slaughters a cow and sells it,
and it became known that it is a tereifa —
what they ate, they ate,
and what they did not eat —
they return the meat to him,
and he returns the money to them.
If they sold it to gentiles, or threw it to the dogs —
they pay the value of a tereifa.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכֵן הַשּׁוֹחֵט אֶת הַפָּרָה וּמְכָרָהּ וְנוֹדַע שֶׁהִיא טְרֵפָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel second case in the same משנה
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Leftover טרפה meat goes back to the seller for a refund. Meat the buyers already used for benefit is paid for at the טרפה price.

steps.title: A ברייתא: selling food that turns out to be forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא with three cases: meat that turns out to be בכור, produce that turns out to be טבל, and wine that turns out to be יין נסך. In each case, what was eaten was eaten, and the seller refunds the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if someone sells meat to his friend and it turns out to be meat of a בכור, or produce that turns out to be טבל, or wine that turns out to be יין נסך, what they ate, they ate, and he must return the money to them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens its discussion of the משנה by quoting a ברייתא. The ברייתא applies the rule 'what they ate, they ate, and he refunds the money' to three kinds of forbidden food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא widens the משנה's בכור rule to טבל and יין נסך. In every case the buyers were tricked into eating something forbidden, so the seller must refund them even for what they already ate. This ברייתא sets up the גמרא's next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: The Rabbis taught (introduces a ברייתא)
Produce not yet tithed
Wine used in idol worship
And it turned out to be

phrases.english: GEMARA: The Rabbis taught:
One who sells meat to his fellow
and it turned out to be meat of a firstborn,
produce, and it turned out to be untithed,
wine, and it turned out to be libation wine —
what they ate, they ate,
and he must return the money to them.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנוּ רַבָּנַן הַמּוֹכֵר בָּשָׂר לַחֲבֵירוֹ וְנִמְצָא בְּשַׂר בְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that extends the משנה's בכור rule to other forbidden foods
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A seller of forbidden food (בכור, טבל, יין נסך) refunds the buyers, even for what they already ate.

steps.title: Repulsive foods get a full refund; non-repulsive foods get a reduced refund
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says that for foods people find disgusting, the seller refunds all the money. For foods people do not find disgusting, he subtracts the value of what was eaten. He then lists which foods fall into each group.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר says: For foods that a person is disgusted by, the seller gives back all the money. For foods that a person is not disgusted by, the seller subtracts their value from the refund. The disgusting foods are נבילות, טריפות, שקצים, and רמשים. The non-disgusting foods are בכורות, טבלים, and יין נסך.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר adds a condition to the ברייתא from step 15. It decides how much of the refund the seller must give back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If a buyer ate something disgusting, we assume he got no real enjoyment from it, so he gets every coin back. If he ate something normal-tasting, like ordinary meat, produce, or wine, he did enjoy it. So the seller may subtract the value of that enjoyment. This narrows the earlier rule that the seller simply 'refunds the money.'

keyTerms.meaning: things a person is disgusted by
he must give back the money
he subtracts (deducts) from the refund
animals that died without proper slaughter, and fatally injured animals
disgusting creatures and creeping creatures

steps.confusionAlert: 'יְנַכֶּה' does not mean the seller pays nothing. He still refunds the money, but subtracts the value of the benefit the buyer got from eating.

phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar says:
items that a person is disgusted by —
he must return to them the money,
and items that a person is not disgusted by —
he deducts for them the value (of what they enjoyed).

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁהַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן:
phrases.english: And these are the items a person is disgusted by:
carcasses and tereifot, repulsive creatures and creeping creatures.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵלּוּ הֵן דְּבָרִים שֶׁאֵין הַנֶּפֶשׁ קָצָה בָּהֶן:
phrases.english: And these are the items a person is not disgusted by:
firstborn animals, untithed produce, and libation wine.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a dissenting/qualifying view to the ברייתא of step 15 about how much is refunded.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Disgusting foods get a full refund. Non-disgusting foods get a refund minus the value of the benefit eaten.

steps.title: Why should the buyer pay anything for a בכור?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the deduction for בכור. The buyer can argue that he caused the seller no loss, since the seller could never have used the בכור himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: About a בכור: let the buyer say to the seller, 'What loss did I cause you?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule that the seller may deduct for a בכור that was eaten.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A deduction only makes sense if the buyer took something of value from the seller. An unblemished בכור is forbidden to the owner (it must go to a כהן and be brought as a קרבן). So eating it took nothing away from the seller. Why, then, should the buyer lose part of his refund?

keyTerms.meaning: let him say to him (introduces an argument the other side could make)
what loss have I caused you?

phrases.english: A firstborn — let him (the buyer) say to him (the seller):
What loss have I caused you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the deduction rule of step 16 as applied to בכור.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's listing of בכור among items where the seller deducts.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A deduction requires that the seller lost something of value. An unblemished בכור was worthless to the seller, so the buyer caused no loss.

steps.title: The meat came from the blemished spot, so the seller could have had it permitted
steps.stepSummary: The rule is needed for a case where the seller sold meat from the blemished part of the animal. If the buyer had not eaten it, the seller could have shown the blemish to an expert and been allowed to eat it. This follows רבי יהודה.
steps.simpleTranslation: No, the ruling is needed for a case where he sold him meat from the place of the blemish. The seller can say: 'If you hadn't eaten it, I would have shown it to an expert, and he would have permitted it to me.' This follows רבי יהודה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. It describes a case where the seller really did lose something when the buyer ate the meat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור with a blemish may be eaten by its owner once an expert confirms the blemish. Here the blemish was on the very piece the buyer ate. Eating it destroyed the evidence, which cost the seller the chance to have it permitted. This works only according to רבי יהודה, who allows an expert to examine a בכור even after it has been slaughtered.

keyTerms.meaning: no, it is needed for (a specific case)
the place of the blemish
I would have shown it (to an expert)
he would have permitted it to him

steps.whyThisMatters: This answer depends on the debate over examining a בכור after slaughter. רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule about בכור only fits the view of רבי יהודה.

phrases.english: No, it is necessary,
for example, where he sold him (meat) from the place of the blemish,
so that he can say to him:
if not for the fact that you ate it,
I would have shown it (to an expert) and he would have permitted it to me,
phrases.notes: The expert would have seen the blemish on this piece of meat.

phrases.english: in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda.
phrases.notes: רבי יהודה allows a בכור to be examined after it was slaughtered.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא, כְּגוֹן דְּזַבֵּין לֵיהּ מִמְּקוֹם מוּמָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17 by narrowing the case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא) and tying it to a specific Tanna's view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A בכור is worthless to the seller, so eating it causes him no loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: In the case of meat from the blemished spot, the seller lost the chance to have it permitted, according to רבי יהודה.

steps.title: טבל could have been tithed, and יין נסך was in a mixture
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא applies the same reasoning to the other two items. The seller could have tithed the טבל and eaten it. The יין נסך case is one where it was mixed with permitted wine, which according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל can still be used for benefit.
steps.simpleTranslation: With טבלים, the seller can say: 'I would have fixed them by tithing and eaten them.' With יין נסך, the case is one where it was in a mixture, and this follows רבן שמעון בן גמליאל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא extends its answer to טבל and יין נסך. It shows that in each case the seller lost something real when the buyer ate the food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: טבל is only forbidden until it is tithed. Once the seller separated the tithes, he could have eaten the rest, so the buyer took something of value. Pure יין נסך is forbidden even for benefit. But when it is mixed into permitted wine, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל allows benefit from the mixture (by selling it to a gentile, minus the value of the forbidden wine). So the seller again lost real value.

keyTerms.meaning: I would have fixed (tithed) it
by way of a mixture
the Tanna who permits benefit from a mixture containing יין נסך

steps.whatToRemember: Under רבי שמעון בן אלעזר's rule, the seller may deduct only when the buyer's eating took away something the seller could really have used. The cases are the blemished בכור (per רבי יהודה), טבל that could have been tithed, and יין נסך in a mixture (per רבן שמעון בן גמליאל).

phrases.english: Untithed produce — (he can say) I would have fixed them (by tithing)
and eaten them,
libation wine — it is a case of a mixture,
and in accordance with Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel.

steps.triggerLanguage: טְבָלִים — הֲוָה מַתְקֵינְנָא לְהוּ וְאָכֵלְנָא לְהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Extends the answer of step 18 to the other two non-repulsive items listed in step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explaining each case so that the seller suffered a real loss
steps.terutzHavaAmina: טבל and יין נסך are forbidden, so eating them took nothing from the seller.
steps.terutzMaskana: The seller could have tithed the טבל. The יין נסך was in a mixture usable per רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. So a deduction is justified.

steps.title: The source for רבן שמעון בן גמליאל on mixed יין נסך
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה. The חכמים forbid all benefit from a cistern of wine that has יין נסך mixed into it. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says the whole cistern may be sold to non-Jews, except for the value of the forbidden wine in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: As we learned in a משנה: If יין נסך fell into a cistern of wine, all of the wine is forbidden for any benefit. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: All of it may be sold to non-Jews, except for the money that matches the value of the יין נסך inside it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the source for what it said in Step 19. It shows that, according to רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, wine mixed with יין נסך still has value, because it can be sold.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 19, the גמרא said the seller lost something real, because mixed יין נסך can still be used for benefit. This משנה proves that claim. Since רבן שמעון בן גמליאל lets the mixture be sold, keeping only the value of the forbidden part off-limits, the seller could have made money from it. So the buyer who drank it did cause him a loss.

keyTerms.meaning: As we learned in a משנה. This introduces a quote from a משנה.
A cistern or pit, here a large wine storage pit.
Forbidden for any benefit, not just for eating or drinking.
The value or money worth of something.

steps.whatToRemember: Steps 17 to 20 make one point. In every case (בכור, טבל, יין נסך), the item could have been worth something to the seller. That is why, according to רבי שמעון בן אלעזר, the seller may deduct the value of what the buyer ate from the refund.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the whole סוגיא of the item that turned out to be forbidden. It shows that the refund rule depends on whether the seller truly lost something.

phrases.english: As we learned: libation wine that fell into a cistern —
all of it is forbidden for benefit.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
all of it may be sold to non-Jews,
except for the value of the libation wine that is in it.
phrases.notes: That portion of the money must be destroyed.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the source for the view of רבן שמעון בן גמליאל that Step 19 relied on.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that mixed יין נסך still has usable value, so the seller suffered a real loss.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in עבודה זרה (74a) about יין נסך that fell into a cistern.

steps.title: הדרן — Closing פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין
steps.stepSummary: The closing formula for פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין.
steps.simpleTranslation: We will return to you, פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין.
steps.whatsHappening: The previous פרק ends here. This is a closing line, not part of any argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying הדרן is the custom when finishing a פרק. It shows we hope to come back and learn it again. Everything after this line belongs to a new פרק.

keyTerms.meaning: We will return to you. This is the closing formula of a פרק.
Sacrificial animals that became disqualified, the name of the previous פרק.

phrases.english: We will return to you, "All disqualified consecrated animals."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the פרק after the final proof in Step 20.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The פרק כל פסולי המוקדשין is complete.

steps.title: New chapter: ear blemishes that permit slaughtering a firstborn
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה lists ear blemishes that permit slaughtering a בכור outside the בית המקדש. They are: a nick in the cartilage (not just the skin), a split, a hole the size of a vetch seed, or a dried-out ear.
steps.simpleTranslation: For these blemishes, one may slaughter the בכור: if its ear was nicked in the cartilage, but not if only the skin was nicked; if the ear was split, even though nothing is missing; if it was pierced with a hole the size of a vetch seed; or if the ear dried out.
steps.whatsHappening: A new פרק begins. The משנה starts listing the blemishes that let a בכור be slaughtered and eaten, beginning with blemishes of the ear.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A בכור with a lasting blemish cannot be brought as a קרבן, but it may be slaughtered and eaten anywhere. The משנה sets exact limits. A nick must reach the firm cartilage, because damage only to the skin does not count. A split counts even if no piece is missing. A hole counts only if it is at least the size of a vetch seed.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה. This marks the start of the משנה text.
Blemishes or physical defects.
A firstborn male animal, which is holy and given to a כהן.
Cartilage, the firm part of the ear.
It was split.
A vetch seed, a small legume used as a size measure.

steps.confusionAlert: Slaughtering here does not mean bringing the animal as a קרבן. A blemished בכור can no longer be offered. These blemishes are what allow it to be slaughtered and eaten as regular meat.

phrases.english: MISHNA: For these blemishes
one may slaughter the firstborn:
if its ear was nicked in the cartilage,
but not if only the skin was nicked,

phrases.aramaic: נִסְדְּקָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא חָסְרָה,
phrases.english: if it was split, even though nothing is missing,
if it was pierced with a hole the size of a vetch seed,
or if it dried out.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ עַל אֵלּוּ מוּמִין שׁוֹחֲטִין אֶת הַבְּכוֹר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new פרק after the הדרן.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A בכור may be slaughtered for these ear blemishes: a nick in the cartilage (not the skin), a split, a hole the size of a vetch seed, or a dried-out ear.

steps.title: Defining a dried-out ear
steps.stepSummary: The משנה defines a dried ear as one that does not give out a drop of blood when pierced. רבי יוסי בן המשולם says it must be so dry that it crumbles.
steps.simpleTranslation: What counts as a dried-out ear? Any ear that, when pierced, does not give out a drop of blood. רבי יוסי בן המשולם says: a dried-out ear means one so dry that it crumbles.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה explains the last item on its list, the dried-out ear. It gives two opinions on how dry the ear must be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion uses a simple test: pierce the ear, and if no blood comes out, it counts as dried. רבי יוסי בן המשולם sets a stricter standard. The ear must be so dry that it crumbles when touched.

keyTerms.meaning: Which one is it? / What counts as?
Dried out.
A drop of blood.
It crumbles.

phrases.english: What counts as dried out?

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל שֶׁתִּנָּקֵב וְאֵינָהּ מוֹצִיאָה טִיפַּת דָּם.
phrases.english: Any ear that, when pierced, does not give out a drop of blood.
Rabbi Yosei ben HaMeshullam says:
Dried out means that it crumbles.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Defines the last blemish listed in Step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: According to the תנא קמא, an ear is dried if piercing it draws no blood. According to רבי יוסי בן המשולם, it must be dry enough to crumble.

steps.title: Why do other blemishes count if the verse mentions only lame and blind?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why these ear blemishes permit slaughtering a בכור. The פסוק only mentions a lame animal and a blind one.
steps.simpleTranslation: Why? The פסוק only says 'lame' and 'blind'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens the new פרק by challenging the משנה. It asks where the תורה allows other blemishes, such as ear blemishes, to permit slaughtering a בכור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק about a blemished בכור names only פסח (lame) and עור (blind). So how can the משנה add ear blemishes that the פסוק does not mention? The next step will answer from another phrase in the same פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: The start of the גמרא's discussion of the משנה.
Why?
A lame animal.
A blind animal.
It is written in the פסוק.

phrases.english: GEMARA: Why?
Only "lame" and "blind" are written!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה's list of ear blemishes from Steps 22 and 23.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's rule that ear blemishes permit slaughtering a בכור.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק names only lame and blind. That suggests only those blemishes, or ones like them, count, so the source for ear blemishes is unclear.

steps.title: The Torah also says 'if there is a blemish in it'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers the question from Step 24: besides lame and blind, the פסוק also has a general phrase about any blemish.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is also written: 'If there be a blemish in it.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers why ear blemishes count. It points out that the פסוק does not only list 'lame or blind'; it also says generally 'כי יהיה בו מום'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 asked how we know about blemishes beyond lameness and blindness. The answer is that the פסוק also contains a broad phrase, 'any blemish', so other blemishes can be included too.

keyTerms.meaning: A physical blemish that disqualifies an animal from the מזבח
It is also written

phrases.english: It is also written
'If there be a blemish in it'
phrases.notes: דברים טו:כא, said about a בכור

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 24
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to an additional, broader phrase in the פסוק
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Only lameness and blindness are mentioned, so only they should permit slaughtering a בכור
steps.terutzMaskana: The general phrase 'כי יהיה בו מום' includes other blemishes

steps.title: Maybe it is a general-then-specific pattern, limited to lame and blind
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: 'any blemish' followed by 'lame or blind' is a כלל ופרט, and that pattern limits the law to the specifics.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: 'If there be a blemish in it' is a general statement, and 'lame or blind' is a specific detail. With a general statement followed by a detail, the general includes only what is in the detail. So lame and blind count, and nothing else.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the answer. It says the order of the words in the פסוק could actually limit the law to lameness and blindness only.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There is a rule of דרשה called כלל ופרט. When a general word is followed by specific examples, the general word only covers those examples. If that rule applies here, the broad phrase adds nothing, and ear blemishes would not count.

keyTerms.meaning: A general statement in a פסוק
A specific detail in a פסוק

keyTerms.term: כְּלָל וּפְרָט אֵין בַּכְּלָל אֶלָּא מָה שֶׁבַּפְּרָט
keyTerms.meaning: When a general statement is followed by a detail, only the detail is included
Lame
Blind

steps.confusionAlert: Here the general phrase does not widen the law. In a plain כלל ופרט, it shrinks down to just the listed examples.

phrases.english: But say: 'If there be a blemish in it' is a generalization,
'lame or blind' is a detail,
and with a generalization and a detail, the generalization includes nothing
except what is in the detail;
lame and blind, yes,
anything else, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of Step 25
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that 'כי יהיה בו מום' includes additional blemishes
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the rule of כלל ופרט, the general phrase is limited to the listed details, so only lame and blind would count

steps.title: A second general phrase makes it general-specific-general
steps.stepSummary: 'כל מום רע' generalizes again, creating a כלל ופרט וכלל. This includes anything similar to the detail: blemishes that are visible and do not heal.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Any bad blemish': it generalized again. With general, specific, general, you include only things similar to the detail. Just as the detail is made up of blemishes that are visible and do not heal, so too all blemishes that are visible and do not heal are included.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the פסוק adds another general phrase after the specifics. That changes the pattern and widens what counts as a blemish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When the pattern is general, specific, general, we include things that share the key features of the specific examples. Lameness and blindness are both visible and permanent. So any visible, permanent blemish counts, and ear blemishes can now be included.

keyTerms.meaning: General, specific, general: include only things similar to the detail
Similar to the detail
Visible, exposed blemishes
They do not grow back or heal

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the basic rule for what counts as a blemish for a בכור: it must be visible and permanent.

phrases.english: 'Any bad blemish': it generalized again,
so it is a generalization, a detail, and a generalization:

phrases.aramaic: אִי אַתָּה דָן אֶלָּא כְּעֵין הַפְּרָט;
phrases.english: you may only derive things similar to the detail;
just as the detail is clearly
blemishes that are visible and do not heal,

phrases.aramaic: אַף כֹּל מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי וְאֵינָן חוֹזְרִין.
phrases.english: so too, all blemishes that are visible and do not heal.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 26
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframes the פסוק as a different דרשה pattern
steps.terutzHavaAmina: It is a כלל ופרט, limited to lame and blind
steps.terutzMaskana: It is a כלל ופרט וכלל, including all visible, permanent blemishes

steps.title: Why not also require that the blemish stops the animal from working?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests a third shared feature: lameness and blindness both stop the animal from working. If that were required, the משנה's ear-nick blemish would not count.
steps.simpleTranslation: But say: just as the detail is blemishes that are visible, stop the animal from its work, and do not heal, so too all blemishes must be visible, stop it from its work, and not heal. Then why did we learn: 'its ear was nicked in the cartilage, not in the skin'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the list of shared features. It asks why we leave out a feature that lame and blind animals also share, namely that they cannot work.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If we copy every shared feature of the detail, we should also require that the blemish stops the animal from working. But a nicked ear does not stop an animal from working, and the משנה still counts it as a blemish. So that stricter reading seems to contradict the משנה.

keyTerms.meaning: Stops the animal from doing its work
Why then did we learn (in the משנה)?
Cartilage

phrases.english: But say: just as the detail is clearly

phrases.aramaic: מוּמִין שֶׁבַּגָּלוּי, וּבוֹטֵל מִמְּלַאכְתּוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ חוֹזֵר,
phrases.english: blemishes that are visible, stop it from its work, and do not heal,
so too all: blemishes that are visible,
that stop it from its work, and do not heal.
Why then did we learn:
'its ear was nicked from the cartilage'
'and not from the skin'?
phrases.notes: This blemish does not stop the animal from working

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the definition derived in Step 27
steps.kashyaTarget: The list of features derived from the detail
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Another shared feature, stopping the animal from work, should also be required. That would contradict the משנה's ear-nick blemish.

steps.title: The word 'any' adds extra inclusion
steps.stepSummary: 'כל מום רע' is a ריבוי, an amplification, so blemishes that do not stop work are included too.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Any bad blemish' is an amplification.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the word 'כל' (any) widens the law beyond the normal similar-to-the-detail rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because the word 'כל' is a ריבוי, we do not need every feature of lameness and blindness. So a blemish that does not stop the animal from working, like a nicked ear, still counts.

keyTerms.meaning: An amplification: a word that adds more cases
Any bad blemish

phrases.english: 'Any bad blemish' is an amplification,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reads a word in the פסוק as a ריבוי
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The blemish must also stop the animal from working
steps.terutzMaskana: The word 'כל' widens the law, so that requirement is dropped

steps.title: Then hidden blemishes should count too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: if 'כל' widens the law, hidden blemishes should also count. It then begins citing a משנה about gum blemishes, which seems to say otherwise.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, hidden blemishes too? Then why did we learn: 'the outer gums that were damaged or scratched, and the inner ones that were uprooted'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the ריבוי. If it widens the law, it might also include hidden blemishes. The challenge, based on a משנה about gums, continues on the next עמוד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If 'כל' cancels the work requirement, why not also cancel the visible requirement? The משנה treats outer and inner gums differently: outer gums count when merely damaged, but inner gums count only when uprooted. This suggests a merely damaged hidden spot is not a blemish.
